lessons.title: Traveling and the gather step
lessons.objective: Explain the gather step and why travel calls confuse everyone.

payload.prompt: A handler gathers the ball, then takes two steps and shoots. Traveling?

options.text: Yes, always a travel
No, the gather step doesn't count against the two-step limit
Only if both feet land at the same time

explanation.correct: The gather, where the player secures the ball, is not counted as a step. Two more steps are then legal, so the footwork can look like three, and that is why travel calls confuse everyone.
explanation.incorrect: Securing the ball (the gather) is free. After it, a player may take two steps before shooting or passing. A third step after the gather is when it becomes a travel.
explanation.sayThisLine: Gather, step one, step two. That's legal.

payload.prompt: A handler does a euro step: left, then right, evading the defender. Legal?

options.text: No, you can only step in one direction
Yes, as long as the steps come after the gather
Only if the defender is moving

explanation.correct: Correct. The euro step is legal in the NBA and college. First step one way, second step the other way, both after the gather.
explanation.incorrect: The euro step is legal. The ball handler takes one step to one side then one to the other, both counted as the two allowed steps after the gather.
explanation.sayThisLine: Euro step is two steps in different directions. It's legal.

payload.prompt: A player catches the ball and pivots on their right foot, rotating 360 degrees. Legal?

options.text: Yes, a pivot foot can rotate any amount
No, you can only pivot 180 degrees
Only in the post

explanation.correct: A player holding the ball can spin on the pivot foot as many times as they like. The foot just cannot slide, drag or lift and come back down before the ball is passed, shot or dribbled.
explanation.incorrect: Once a player holds the ball, one foot becomes the pivot, and it can turn in place as much as the player wants. Only lifting it and putting it down again, or dragging it, is a travel.
explanation.sayThisLine: Plant a pivot foot and you can spin all day.

payload.prompt: Ball handler gathers, then takes three more steps without dribbling. Traveling?

scene.alt: A ball handler secures the ball and then takes three more steps toward the basket without dribbling.

explanation.correct: After the gather, two steps are the limit. A third step with no dribble is a travel, and here the player took three.
explanation.incorrect: The gather is free and two steps after it are legal. Three more steps without a dribble is one too many, so the whistle is deserved.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Gather, one, two. That third step is a travel."

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: He traveled for sure, too many steps.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The player took too many steps without dribbling.
The player stepped out of bounds.
The player took exactly two steps after the catch.
The player used the wrong pivot foot for a pass.

payload.translation: After catching the ball, the player took more than two steps without dribbling it, which is a violation.

followUps.why: It shows you know the gather is free, and it invites her to explain what she saw.

followUps.line: Do refs call it the same way every time?
followUps.why: Fans argue about travel consistency all the time, so this keeps the talk going.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Travel calls are famously inconsistent; saying 'that looked like a travel' is safe.

lessons.title: Dribbling violations
lessons.objective: Tell a double dribble from a carry from a clean dribble.

payload.prompt: A dribbler crosses the ball from the right hand to the left without stopping. Violation?

scene.alt: A dribbler bounces the ball with the right hand, then crosses it over and keeps bouncing with the left hand.

explanation.correct: Legal. Changing hands is fine as long as the dribble never stops. A double dribble needs a stop, or both hands on the ball at once, before the dribbling resumes.
explanation.incorrect: Switching hands mid-dribble is a normal crossover. Double dribble means dribbling again after the dribble ended, or dribbling with both hands at the same time.
explanation.sayThisLine: "That crossover was nasty, and completely legal."

payload.prompt: A dribbler palms the ball (lets it rest in their hand) while moving. Violation?

scene.alt: A ball handler holding the ball in their palm while not bouncing it.

explanation.correct: Carrying, or palming, is a dribble violation. The hand has to push the ball down from on top; once it turns under or rests beneath the ball, the dribble has ended.
explanation.incorrect: A legal dribble pushes the ball from above and lets it bounce. When the hand slides under the ball and carries it along, that is a carry and the other team gets the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: "He carried it. The hand was under the ball."

payload.prompt: A handler brings the ball into the front court, then dribbles it back across half court. Violation?

scene.alt: A player advancing the ball into the opponent's half, then dribbling back across half court.

explanation.correct: Once the offense has brought the ball into the frontcourt, it cannot go back over half court. Doing it is an over-and-back, a turnover on the team with the ball.
explanation.incorrect: After the ball and the dribbler get into the frontcourt, the offense may not take it back across the half-court line. The defense, however, can knock it back without a violation.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Over and back. He took it back across half."

payload.prompt: A player dribbles, picks up the ball, holds it, then dribbles again. Violation?

scene.alt: A dribbler stopping the dribble, cradling the ball, then resuming the dribble.

explanation.correct: Once a player catches the ball with both hands or holds it, the dribble is over. Starting a new dribble is a double dribble, unless someone else touched the ball in between.
explanation.incorrect: After a player ends the dribble, the only legal moves are to pass, shoot or pivot. Bouncing the ball again without anyone else touching it is a double dribble.
explanation.sayThisLine: "He picked it up and dribbled again. That is a double."

payload.prompt: Which signal means double dribble?

image.alt: Illustration of a referee with both palms facing down, patting up and down in front of the body as if dribbling with two hands.

options.text: Both palms patting up and down
Fists rolling over each other
Both thumbs pointing up
A closed fist raised overhead

explanation.correct: The referee pats the air with both palms, like someone dribbling with two hands. It is the double-dribble signal.
explanation.incorrect: Double dribble looks like what it is: two hands patting a pretend ball. Rolling fists mean traveling, thumbs up mean a jump ball, and a raised fist stops the clock for a foul.

payload.prompt: When the ref sees a player carrying the ball, what happens?

options.text: Award a free throw
Call a turnover; the other team gets the ball
Give a technical foul

explanation.correct: A carry is a violation, not a foul, so there are no free throws. The ball is simply awarded to the other team for an inbound.
explanation.incorrect: Violations such as carrying are turnovers: no free throws and no technical foul, just a throw-in for the other team at the nearest spot.

payload.prompt: Match the violation to the time limit it involves.

pairs.definition: Offensive player stays in the paint for more than 3 seconds while their team has the ball.
Inbounder takes over 5 seconds to get the ball in play or closely guarded player holds the ball over 5 seconds.
Team fails to get the ball across half court within 8 seconds (ten in college).
Team fails to get a shot off before the shot clock expires: 24 sec NBA/WNBA, 30 in college.

explanation.summary: These clock rules keep the game moving and prevent endless stalling in any area.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three seconds in the lane, eight to cross half, 24 on the shot clock.

payload.prompt: A big sits in the lane two seconds, steps fully out, then back in two more. Violation?

scene.alt: An offensive player stands in the painted lane for two seconds, steps out with both feet, then steps back in while the ball stays on the perimeter.

explanation.correct: Legal. The three-second count only builds while the player stays in the lane. Leaving with both feet resets it, which is why bigs pop in and out.
explanation.incorrect: The violation needs three straight seconds in the lane while the offense has the ball in the frontcourt. Stepping out with both feet restarts the count.
explanation.sayThisLine: "He keeps stepping out of the lane so the three-second count resets."

payload.prompt: A team takes 10 seconds to get the ball across half court in the NBA. Violation?

scene.alt: A team slowly advancing the ball down court past the half-court line.

explanation.correct: In the NBA a team has eight seconds to get the ball across half court. Ten is too slow, so the ball goes to the other team. College allows ten.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA and WNBA allow eight seconds to reach the frontcourt, and college allows ten. Ten seconds in the NBA is a violation and a turnover.
explanation.sayThisLine: "They ran out of time getting it over half court."

payload.prompt: A shot leaves the hands before the shot clock hits zero, then misses everything. Violation?

scene.alt: A late heave leaves the shooter's hand with the shot clock almost at zero and sails past the basket without touching the rim.

explanation.correct: To beat the shot clock, the ball must leave the hand in time and then hit the rim. An airball does not reset anything, so it is a shot-clock violation.
explanation.incorrect: Releasing in time is only half the rule. The shot also has to touch the rim or go in. A shot that touches nothing is a violation, and the ball goes to the other team.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Airball with the clock running out is a shot-clock violation."

payload.prompt: Complete the clock rules for the NBA.
payload.template: A team has {{eight}} seconds to get the ball across half court and {{twentyfour}} seconds to shoot it.

explanation.correct: Right. Eight to cross half, 24 to shoot in the NBA. College is ten and 30.
explanation.incorrect: NBA rules: eight seconds to get across half court, 24 seconds for a shot. These times differ in college and the WNBA.

lessons.title: Personal and shooting fouls
lessons.objective: Sort fouls by type and explain the and-one.

payload.prompt: A defender pushes an offensive player away from the ball. What foul is this?

options.text: Shooting foul
Personal foul
Technical foul

explanation.correct: Pushing, holding or hitting a player who is not in the act of shooting is a personal foul. It counts toward the player's six and the team's foul total.
explanation.incorrect: It is not a shooting foul, because no shot was going up, and it is not a technical, which is about conduct. Illegal contact away from a shot is a plain personal foul.

payload.prompt: A defender fouls a shooter and the shot goes in. What happens?

options.text: The basket doesn't count
The basket counts and the player shoots one free throw (and-one)
The basket counts and the player shoots two free throws

explanation.correct: A made shot with a foul on it is an and-one: the points count and the shooter gets one bonus free throw. Fans call it a three-point play when the shot was a two.
explanation.incorrect: A foul does not erase a good basket. The shot counts, and the shooter gets exactly one extra free throw, the and-one, because the foul cost them a chance at the free point.

payload.prompt: A player gets their sixth personal foul in the NBA. What happens?

options.text: They sit out one quarter
They foul out and cannot play the rest of the game
They lose two free throws

explanation.correct: A sixth personal foul disqualifies a player in the NBA, so they sit for good and a teammate subs in. College uses five. Ejection is a separate thing, for flagrant or technical fouls.
explanation.incorrect: In the NBA a sixth personal foul disqualifies the player for the rest of the game, including overtime. There is no timed penalty and no free-throw penalty.

payload.prompt: Order an and-one, from contact to the free throw.

items.text: A defender hits the shooter during the shot.
items.why: The contact happens as the shot goes up.
A good shot is not cancelled by the foul.

items.text: The ref counts the basket and awards one free throw.
items.why: The whistle and the signal come with the made shot.

items.text: The shooter takes the free throw.
items.why: The bonus attempt is the last step.

explanation.correct: Contact, a good shot, then the ref counts the basket and sends the shooter to the line for one more. That extra point is what makes it an and-one.
explanation.incorrect: An and-one runs in this order: contact on the shooter, the shot goes in, the ref counts it and awards one free throw, and then the free throw is shot.

payload.prompt: How many personal fouls does a player need in the NBA before fouling out?

explanation.correct: Six fouls in the NBA and WNBA. College is five.
explanation.incorrect: A player fouls out at six personal fouls in the NBA and WNBA. College is five fouls.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: We're in the bonus, so any foul sends us to the line.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The other team has used up its fouls, so each new foul means free throws
A player just made a three-pointer and gets extra points
The team has earned a reward for playing defense
Subsequent fouls will be non-shooting fouls

payload.translation: The other team has piled up team fouls this quarter (four in the NBA), so their next foul, and every one after, sends his team to the line for two shots.

followUps.line: How many fouls have they got?
followUps.why: It shows you know the bonus is a team count, and it is an easy question to answer.

followUps.line: Does that count reset every quarter?
followUps.why: It checks your picture of how the bonus works, and it does reset each quarter.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking 'how many team fouls did they have?' is always safe.

lessons.title: Free throws, the bonus and techs
lessons.objective: Explain bonus, technical, flagrant and intentional fouls.

payload.prompt: Match the foul type to its definition.

pairs.definition: A conduct foul for arguing, taunting or delay, not ordinary contact. The other team shoots one free throw.
Unnecessary contact, more than a normal foul. Two free throws and the ball for the fouled team.
Unnecessary and excessive contact. The fouler is ejected; two free throws and the ball for the other team.
A deliberate foul to stop the clock or the play, not an attempt to play the ball. It can cost extra free throws.

explanation.summary: A technical is about conduct, a flagrant is contact that goes too far, and an intentional foul is a deliberate stop. Each has its own penalty.
explanation.sayThisLine: "That was a flagrant. It was more than a normal foul."

payload.prompt: A coach yells at the referee, 'That's a terrible call!' The ref points at the coach. What is called?

options.text: Technical foul on the coach
Unsportsmanlike conduct on the player
Delay of game

explanation.correct: A technical foul is for conduct, and a coach who shouts at the ref can get one. The other team shoots a free throw, and a second technical means ejection.
explanation.incorrect: Delay of game is about stalling, and unsportsmanlike conduct on a player is not what the coach did. A coach who argues or shows up an official is given a technical foul.

payload.prompt: The other team has four fouls this NBA quarter. It commits another. What happens?

options.text: Play continues with a throw-in and no free throws
Your team shoots two free throws
Your team shoots one free throw and keeps the ball

explanation.correct: After four team fouls in a quarter, the fifth and every later foul sends the other team to the line for two shots, even when nobody was shooting.
explanation.incorrect: In the NBA, four team fouls in a quarter put a team in the penalty. Its next foul gives the opponent two free throws whether or not the player was shooting.

payload.prompt: A defender elbows an offensive player hard while driving. This is ruled flagrant-2. What is the consequence?

options.text: Two free throws and the fouled player keeps the ball
Two free throws, the fouled team gets possession, and the defender is ejected
One technical free throw and a technical is charged

explanation.correct: A flagrant-2 is the top tier: the defender is thrown out, the fouled player shoots two free throws, and their team keeps the ball afterward.
explanation.incorrect: A flagrant-2 is more than a technical or a standard foul. The fouler is ejected, the fouled team shoots two free throws and then gets the ball back.

payload.prompt: Complete the NBA bonus foul rule.
payload.template: After a team commits {{count}} fouls in an NBA quarter, every foul after that gives the opponent {{shots}} free throws.

explanation.correct: Four team fouls in a quarter puts a team in the penalty, so its fifth and later fouls mean two free throws each. The count starts over every quarter.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA penalty starts after four team fouls in a quarter, and each foul after that means two free throws. College counts differently, by half, and uses seven and ten.

lessons.title: Charge or block?
lessons.objective: Judge charge vs block using position, feet and the restricted-area arc.

payload.prompt: Defender is standing still with feet planted and arms up. An offensive player drives into them. Charge or block?

scene.alt: A stationary defender with feet planted, arms raised. An offensive player collides into the defender's chest.

explanation.correct: The defender got to the spot first and was set, feet planted in a legal guarding position, before the driver made contact. That makes the contact the driver's fault: a charge.
explanation.incorrect: When a defender is already set in a legal spot and the offensive player runs into them, the offensive player is responsible. A block is the call when the defender is still moving or late to the spot.

payload.prompt: A help defender stands inside the restricted arc. A driver runs into him. Charge?

scene.alt: A help defender stands set inside the small arc under the basket, and a driver from the wing runs into him.

explanation.correct: A secondary, or help, defender standing in the restricted-area arc cannot draw a charge. The arc keeps rim collisions from being decided by who falls down.
explanation.incorrect: The restricted-area rule protects drivers from help defenders who slide in under the rim. Contact there is not a charge on the driver, and the defender may even be called for a block.

payload.prompt: A set defender keeps both hands straight up. A driver runs into his chest. Foul on the defender?

scene.alt: A defender stands still with both arms straight up above the shoulders. A driver runs into his chest.

explanation.correct: A defender who stays in his own space with hands straight up is playing by the verticality rule. If the driver runs into him, the responsibility is on the driver.
explanation.incorrect: Verticality lets a defender go straight up without penalty. Reaching out or leaning into the driver would be a foul, but standing tall and still is not.

payload.prompt: Tap the restricted-area arc under the basket.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram. The rim sits near the bottom edge with a small semicircle around it. The lane rises above it, with the elbow at each top corner of the lane and a wing out to the side.

explanation.correct: The restricted area is the small semicircle right under the rim, 4 feet out. A help defender standing in it cannot draw a charge.
explanation.incorrect: That is another spot on the floor. The restricted area is the small semicircle directly under the basket, where a help defender cannot draw a charge.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: That should have been a charge. He was set before the driver got there.

payload.question: What is Casey saying?

options.text: The defender was late, so a block was the right call
The defender got in place first, so the driver caused the contact
The defender fouled the driver while the ball was in the air
The driver took too many steps before contact

payload.translation: Casey thinks the defender beat the driver to the spot and was set, so the contact was the driver's responsibility: an offensive foul, not a block on the defender.

followUps.line: Was he outside the restricted area?
followUps.why: Location can change the call, so it is a smart question to ask.

followUps.line: Did his feet get set in time?
followUps.why: Timing of the defender's position is the heart of a charge call.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Charge versus block is one of the most argued calls in the sport. Saying 'I thought he was set' is a fair, honest take.

lessons.title: Goaltending and basket interference
lessons.objective: Know when a ball on the way down or up can no longer be touched.

payload.prompt: A shot is heading downward toward the rim when a defender taps it away. Goaltending?

scene.alt: A shot falling toward the basket is touched by a defender before it hits the rim.

explanation.correct: Once a shot is on its way down toward the basket, above the rim and with a chance to score, nobody may touch it. The shooting team is awarded the points.
explanation.incorrect: A shot on its downward path toward the rim is off limits. Touching it is goaltending, and if a defender does it, the basket is counted as good.

payload.prompt: A shot is resting on the rim when a defender flicks it off. Violation?

scene.alt: A ball sits on the rim while a defender's hand reaches up and knocks it off.

explanation.correct: Once the ball is on the rim, it is the basket's to settle. Touching it is basket interference, and the shooting team is awarded the points.
explanation.incorrect: A ball on the rim is still a live shot. Knocking it off is basket interference, which is goaltending's close cousin.

payload.prompt: A miss bounces far from the rim and drops toward the floor. Can a defender grab it?

scene.alt: A missed shot bounces well away from the rim and falls toward the floor, where a defender reaches for it.

explanation.correct: Legal. Once a miss has bounced clear of the rim with no chance to score, it is a live rebound and anyone can grab it.
explanation.incorrect: Goaltending only protects a shot that still has a chance to score. A rebound that has left the basket area is a free ball.

payload.prompt: Which of these is basket interference?

options.text: Grabbing the rim while a shot is in the air
Jumping to block a shot on its way up
Rebounding a miss that has left the rim area
Contesting a shot with a hand in the shooter's face

explanation.correct: Grabbing or shaking the rim or backboard while a shot is live can change where the ball goes, so it is basket interference. A blocked or rebounded ball is normal play.
explanation.incorrect: Blocking a shot on its way up, rebounding a clear miss and a hand in the face are all ordinary defense. Basket interference means touching the rim, the net or the backboard so as to affect a live shot.

payload.prompt: A defender reaches up through the net and touches the ball. What happens?

options.text: The basket is waved off
The shooting team is awarded the basket
The defense gets the ball at the baseline

explanation.correct: Defensive basket interference is a violation, so the shooting team is awarded the points. Reaching up through the net from below is never allowed.
explanation.incorrect: The defense cannot cancel a shot by touching it from under the net. The violation is on the defender and the shooting team gets the points. Only an offensive player's interference wipes out a basket.

lessons.title: Replay, challenges and the L2M
lessons.objective: Explain replay review, coach challenges and the last-two-minute report.

payload.prompt: Which signal stops the clock for a foul?

image.alt: Illustration of a referee with one closed fist raised overhead, the first signal given when a foul is called.

options.text: A closed fist raised overhead
Both arms swept out to the sides
Both palms held flat in front of the chest
One hand waved over the head

explanation.correct: The referee raises a closed fist to stop the clock when a foul is called. After that come the signals for the type of foul and the number of the player.
explanation.incorrect: A foul starts with a raised closed fist, which stops the clock. The signals that show which foul it was, and who committed it, come afterward.

payload.prompt: What hand signal do referees use to call a timeout?

image.alt: Illustration of a referee holding one hand flat across the fingertips of the other, forming a T.

options.text: One hand flat across the other, forming a T
One finger pointing up
Open hand wave across chest
One arm extended to the side

explanation.correct: The T, one hand flat against the fingertips of the other, is the universal sign for a timeout, like the one your coach calls or a player asks for.
explanation.incorrect: A timeout is signaled by forming a T with the hands: one hand flat across the fingertips of the other. Pointing and waving signals mean other things.

payload.prompt: How do referees signal a jump ball?

image.alt: Illustration of a referee with both thumbs pointing up, fists closed, arms raised in front of the chest.

options.text: Both thumbs pointing up
One arm pointing straight up
Arms moving in a circle
Both hands clasped together

explanation.correct: Two thumbs up signals a jump ball, meaning a tie-up. The possession arrow settles who gets the ball.
explanation.incorrect: A jump ball, or tie-up, is signaled with both thumbs up. One arm straight up or waving arms mean other things.

payload.prompt: A coach successfully challenges a foul call in the NBA. Can they challenge again later?

options.text: No, one challenge per game
Yes, they get a second challenge
Only if the second challenge is in the final two minutes

explanation.correct: Under the current NBA rule, a coach has one challenge per game, and a successful one earns a second. A coach needs a timeout in hand to challenge, so it is a real cost.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA lets a coach challenge a call once, and a successful challenge earns a second. The rule has been tweaked before, so check the current version if the details matter.

payload.prompt: What is the NBA's Last-Two-Minute (L2M) report?

options.text: A live feed of player statistics in the final minutes
An official report released after close games reviewing the calls and non-calls in the final two minutes
A coach's challenge review system

explanation.correct: The league reviews the calls, and missed calls, from the closing minutes of tight games and publishes its verdicts. Fans use it to settle arguments about the refs.
explanation.incorrect: The L2M report is not a live feed or a coaching tool. It is the league's after-the-fact review of calls in the last two minutes of close games, published for transparency.
